tips: Missions spend energy - check your resource bar before you sail out.
Jobs cost no energy and pay gold - remember: you can't start a mission or training while working.
Training improves attributes with training points - refill them with gold if needed.
The arena spends fight points and awards fame - come back after a refill.
Dungeons have multiple stages; clearing them fills your bestiary.
On your ship you grow crew, treasury, and upgrades - and fight in ship battles.
Quests and titles reward regular play: claim pending rewards often.
The daily bonus resets if you miss a day - log in every day.
Boosters temporarily empower missions, work, energy, or combat.
Diamonds and coupons are premium shortcuts - gold and loot also come from normal play.

krypta.name: Sunken Crypt
krypta.desc: Dark ruins of a pirate graveyard where mist rises over sunken tombs and undead corsairs watch from broken masts. The Sunken Crypt is the archipelago's first dungeon - ten stages of salt, bone, and the Lich Admiral's drowned ambition.

kraken.name: Kraken's Lair
kraken.desc: Damp tunnels beneath the waves where the kraken's echo bounces off stone and tentacles cut through the dark. Ten stages lead from sentry tentacles to the Heart of the Kraken - the second dungeon in the island chain.

forteca.name: Blackbeard's Fortress
forteca.desc: Blackbeard's abandoned stronghold where gunpowder and gold soaked into the beams and his echo still rules the halls. Clear ten stages of crew, shades, and cannon fire to face the captain himself.

wulkan.name: Davy Jones' Volcano
wulkan.desc: Davy Jones's Volcano - gateway to hellish depths where lava pulses like a cursed heart and drowned souls cry from below. Ten ash-choked stages climb toward the Herald who speaks for the damned admiral.

palac.name: Poseidon's Palace
palac.desc: Poseidon's Palace - golden chambers beneath the reef where coral columns support a throne of tide and storm. Ten stages of Atlantean guards lead to the Avatar who judges every pirate bold enough to enter.

bestiaryPage.title: Bestiary
bestiaryPage.subtitle: A living catalog of dungeon foes across the archipelago. Defeat an enemy to unlock their story - origin, role, sailor gossip, and ties to each dungeon's master.
bestiaryPage.hint: Entries unlock when you defeat an enemy in a dungeon. Return after each stage to fill the bestiary and learn how every guard connects to the boss waiting at stage ten.

lore: The Grave Lantern Keeper tends the first threshold of the Sunken Crypt with a green flame that never goes out. He was once a ship's chaplain who buried pirates at sea - until his own crew drowned him in the hold for preaching mercy to prisoners they meant to kill.

His hood hides a face more waterlogged than human, and his lantern does not light the way forward. It lights the names of the dead carved into wet stone, reminding every intruder that the crypt remembers trespassers.
Pirates say if the lantern flickers when you enter, the Keeper has already written your name in salt. Defeating him is the first proof that this graveyard fights back with more than bones.

Sailors in Port Ash swear the Keeper's lantern still burns on storm nights above the crypt - a green pinprick visible from the reef. Old charts mark the Sunken Crypt as the archipelago's first cursed anchorage; defeating him opens the path the Lich Admiral's drowned fleet once used to bury their dead.

The Barnacle Brawler crawled from a reef where a pirate brig broke apart decades ago. Shells fused to his skin like armor no smith could forge, and each fist carries the weight of tides that never stopped pounding the wreck.
He cannot speak - only roar through a throat full of sand and broken coral. Raiders who survived him claim the barnacles cut their blades as badly as any cutlass.
The bestiary lists the Barnacle Brawler as proof that the sea does not only drown its dead. Sometimes it grows them into something new, hungry, and impossible to ignore.

Dock gossip says barnacles from the Brawler's reef sell for a fortune in Nassau, but no diver returns with a clean haul. He guards the second ring of tombs where the crypt's tide turns violent - a proving ground before the deeper dead awaken for the Vault Revenant's master.

The Gallows Shade hangs where the crypt's ceiling drops low, rope creaking though no beam supports it. He was a mutineer hanged from his own mast and thrown into the burial shafts when the tide rose through the graves.
He has no feet - only the memory of the drop that broke his neck and the cold patience of a punishment that never ended. His fingers are long, grey, and eager to share the noose.
Old captains warn that looking up when you hear rope groan is how the Shade chooses its next victim. The bestiary advises keeping your eyes on the floor - or on your blade.

A mutineer's journal, washed ashore in a corked bottle, describes rope groaning in an empty corridor hours before the Shade appeared. The Gallows Shade marks the crypt's middle descent, where pirates say the Lich Admiral hanged deserters to feed the mist that hides his throne.

The Salt Wraith rises from brine pools that should have dried centuries ago, skin crusted white like harbor frost. He was a smuggler who hid contraband in coffins - until the dead refused to stay buried with his cargo.
Every step leaves crystals that crack like thin ice. His touch burns with the dryness of sun on salt flats, a paradox in a place drowned by the sea.
Sea priests say the Salt Wraith punishes those who profit from graves. Defeating him feels like breaking a curse - and hearing the crypt exhale for the first time in years.

Smugglers once called the Salt Wraith 'the toll collector' - every coffin cargo left a coin of brine on the ledger. He patrols the brine pools that feed the crypt's lower vaults, and sailors claim his defeat thins the fog over the whole sunken graveyard for a week.

The Anchor Knight stands where the crypt narrows into a tomb corridor, shield shaped like a ship's anchor and heavy enough to crush bone. He was a royal marine who hunted pirates - until a curse bound him to guard the very dead he once tried to erase.
His armor weeps rust and seawater. He does not speak oaths anymore; he only counts footsteps until intruders cross the line where mercy ends.
The bestiary records that the Anchor Knight never strikes first. He waits until you prove you want the treasure more than your life - then he reminds you that some doors weigh more than gold.

Royal navy records mention an Anchor Knight lost at the pirate graveyard raid of '68, cursed to guard until 'the sea forgives.' He blocks the corridor to the crypt's treasure tiers - the last checkpoint before rum-soaked halls where the Lich Admiral's treasurer still counts coin.

The Rum Wraith drifts through the ruins of a tavern buried with the crypt, phantom bottles floating around his bloated coat. He was the jolliest bartender in Port Ash - until a poisoned barrel turned his crew into the first bodies interred here.

He laughs without breath and offers drinks that pass through living hands like fog. Those who accept wake days later on the surface with no memory; those who refuse fight a ghost who knows every dirty trick taught in a dockside inn.
Survivors say defeating the Rum Wraith leaves the smell of spilled rum in your hair for a week. The bestiary notes that he is the crypt's cruel joke - death with a smile and a toast.

Tavern songs in Tortuga mock the Rum Wraith's toast, but captains leave a spilled dram at the crypt entrance for luck. His buried tavern sits on the route to the vault antechamber; beat him and dockhands say the air smells less like rot and more like open sea.

The Jelly Widow was a pirate queen who sailed with her husband until a jellyfish bloom swallowed their sloop in a night of phosphorescent horror. She alone walked out of the water - if walking is what the tendrils dragging her bones can be called.
Bioluminescent strands pulse around her like a wedding veil made of venom. She mourns and hunts in the same motion, each strike a memory of the crew she could not save.
The bestiary warns that pity is the deadliest mistake against the Jelly Widow. She does not want comfort. She wants company in the dark.

Fishers off the reef report jellyfish blooms that glow the same green as the Widow's veil - a sign the crypt stirs. She haunts the flooded gallery before the vault, mourning crew the Lich Admiral refused to raise; pity her and the bestiary notes you will join them.

The Lobster Lurker guards a choke point where the crypt floods with cold current, claws clicking like rigging in a gale. He began as a cook's mate who fell overboard into a nest of deep-water lobsters - and climbed back aboard something else entirely.
One arm remains human enough to grip a knife; the other is a chitinous pincer that can snip through chain. He waits in stillness for hours, patient as a trap on the ocean floor.
Pirates who beat him say the fight felt like wrestling the tide itself. The bestiary recommends speed - the Lurker wins every battle that lasts too long.

The Lobster Lurker's choke point appears on smuggler maps as 'the pinch' - no boat passes the crypt's cold current without a fight. Cooks who survived the lair say the Lurker was the admiral's galley terror, kept hungry to warn thieves away from the Lich's hoard.

The Vault Revenant wears a mask of hammered gold over what was once a treasurer's face, coins sewn into rotting finery like buttons. He counted the crypt's plunder for a captain who promised him a share - then sealed him alive with the chest.
He knows the weight of every gem in the vault and the price of every lie told to obtain them. His blows ring like counterfeit coin on stone.
The bestiary says the Vault Revenant is greed made visible. Defeating him does not open the treasury - but it proves you are not here only for gold.

Treasure hunters whisper that the Vault Revenant's mask is real gold, melted from the Lich Admiral's first conquest. He is the final guardian before the throne hall; defeat him and the crypt's bells ring underwater - a sound old captains say the Lich Admiral answers personally.

The Lich Admiral rules the Sunken Crypt from a throne of coral and broken figureheads, crown rusted like an anchor lost to the abyss. He was the greatest pirate admiral of his age - until his fleet sank in a battle so vast the sea still remembers the smoke.

He commands not only magic but the ambition of every captain buried beneath him. His voice is the murmur of water in a drowned bell, and his eyes are lanterns for the dead fleet that sails behind his words.

Defeating the Lich Admiral inscribes a name in legends beside the oldest sea wars. The bestiary closes with a warning: the crypt may yield treasure, but the admiral of the drowned never forgets who dared stand before him.

When the Lich Admiral falls, reef pilots report tides shifting across the whole archipelago for three days - channels open that charts never showed. Crypt Hunter titles are earned here; the drowned fleet's ambition sleeps again, but every captain knows the sea may wake it when greed returns.

The Tentacle Sentry rises from darkness like a living shield, blocking the path of anyone who enters the Kraken's Lair without the sea's permission. Its skin is rough as coral, and its suckers grasp with the precision of a seasoned boarder.
It is the lair's first line of defense - patient, silent, and merciless. It does not ask where you came from. It asks only whether you can survive the first wave that never breaks.

Logs from sunken ships mention Tentacle Sentries appearing just before entire crews vanished. The bestiary advises treating it not as a monster but as a threshold - one you must cross if you wish to know the lair's true face.

Kraken cultists on the outer isles leave fish at cave mouths 'for the sentry' before diving for pearls. The Tentacle Sentry's defeat is the sign pearl divers wait for - only then do they risk the tunnels that echo toward the Heart of the Kraken.

The Juvenile Kraken is still learning to hunt in the cave's narrow tunnels, yet youth does not mean weakness. Young tentacles probe every crack, and its eyes glow with phosphorescent light reflected from wet walls like a lantern in a storm.

It looks less fearsome than its elders, yet its strikes are as quick as a tidal surge - sudden, cold, and hard to predict. Pirates say the Juvenile Kraken attacks like a child that has not yet learned mercy.
The bestiary records that defeating the Juvenile Kraken is a lesson in vigilance. In the lair it is not about seeing the enemy - it is about noticing him before you feel suckers on your ankle.

A juvenile's beak, sold in a Nassau market, supposedly came from this lair - buyers claim it still pulses at night. Young Krakens herd intruders toward the Wide Grasper's corridor; sailors say killing one draws the Lair Warden's attention deeper in.
The Coral Hunter moves among coral colonies, blending into pink and violet hues like a scout in colored fog. Its blows leave stinging wounds like salt in a fresh cut.
Rumor says it collects trophies from every defeated wanderer - shells, coins, even fragments of maps. Its legend grows with every new trace of blood on coral.

In the Kraken's Lair the Coral Hunter acts as a hunter seeking not glory but further proof that the cave belongs to the sea. The bestiary warns: if you see movement among coral, do not trust the colors - trust instinct.

Coral Hunters decorate their lairs with compass shards and earring hooks from dead pirates - trophies the bestiary lists by the dozen. They scout for the Ink Stalker ahead of the heart chamber; defeat this one and the lair's colors grow dull, a sign the Kraken senses you.

The Ink Stalker releases a cloud of black ink that steals direction, courage, and the sense of where water ends and wall begins. In that fog you hear only splashes, breath, and the dry laugh of a creature that knows the tunnel better than you.
Captains say that in such darkness you see your own fears - sinking ships, abandoned crews, nights of hunger. The Ink Stalker does not create illusions. It merely reveals them.

The bestiary records that fighting it is a test of character more than strength. Whoever masters fear may leave the cloud. Whoever hesitates remains in it forever - another tale whispered by sailors at the fire.

Captains teach green hands to count breaths in ink fog: if you reach ten without a strike, the Stalker has chosen mercy. The Stalker guards the miasma vents below the Warden's gate - beat it and veteran divers say the cave air clears enough to see the final descent.

The Abyssal Miasma hangs above the water like toxic vapor born from the sea's wrath and ancient wrecks. Breathing near it dulls the senses, and every movement feels as heavy as diving in armor on the ocean floor.
It has no face or eyes, yet it has intent - to slow the intruder, weaken them, and make them hesitate where the lair is most dangerous. It is a creature that fights through exhaustion.

Old chronicles say the Abyssal Miasma appears where the sea remembers sinkings no one mourned. The bestiary advises: if the air grows thick, do not pause. Either fight at once or withdraw - the miasma offers no third option.

The Abyssal Miasma smells like gunpowder and drowned cargo - old sailors tie scarves over mouths and still fall. It chokes the tunnel before the Wide Grasper's kill zone, weakening crews the Heart of the Kraken prefers half-drowned.

The Wide Grasper spreads its tentacles across the entire corridor, closing every escape route like a living gate. Its strength comes not from speed but from relentless pressure that breaks resistance as a wave breaks a wooden pier.

It does not attack once. It attacks in waves until the opponent loses the rhythm of breath. In a lair where every step echoes, the Wide Grasper can make you feel as if you are fighting the cave itself.

The bestiary notes that defeating the Wide Grasper requires patience and room for error - except in its corridor there is no room for error. Victors say the key is focus: one target, one breath, one strike at a time.

Wide Grasper victims' bones pile in alcoves 'like stacked cannonballs,' according to a salvager's log. This corridor is the Kraken's ribcage in legend - break through and the Phosphor Shade's flashes are the last warning before the Warden and the Heart.

The Spined Spawn is covered in sharp ridges that wound even when it seems to defend passively. Young but already cruel, it attacks in a frenzy as if it must prove its place in the lair hierarchy before older tentacles.
Each blow leaves a mark like claws scraping stone. Pirates who met it claim the Spined Spawn fights not for glory but for fear - its own and yours.
The bestiary considers it the most unpredictable in the entire lair. Not because it is strongest, but because it fights like a being still learning what pain is - and wants to learn it on you.

Spined Spawn scars match the Kraken Slayer title's heraldry in pirate tattoos across Tortuga. The young beast tests intruders for the Heart - too weak and the lair ejects you in ink; strong enough and the Warden rises to measure you properly.
The Phosphor Shade moves in flashes, leaving trails of luminous dust that briefly light the tunnel like comets in a night sky. It is hard to tell where its body ends and the water begins.
Many captains swear they saw it twice before feeling the first blow. The Phosphor Shade fights like an illusion that nonetheless leaves very real wounds.

The bestiary recommends watching not the light but the silence between flashes. There, in that brief pause, you may hear the enemy move. Hearing it early is often the only difference between leaving and disappearing.

Phosphor trails guide lost divers wrong, but also mark safe footing - if you watch the dark between flashes. The Shade dances before the Warden's chamber; sailors bet barrels of rum on whether seeing it twice means death or promotion to Kraken Slayer.

The Lair Warden stands before the final chamber like a living anchor driven into the heart of the cave. It knows every tunnel, shortcut, and echo - because it has listened to them for years, waiting for the next bold soul or fool.

Its presence means the heart of the lair is near, and the price of going deeper will be steep. It says nothing, yet its tentacles arrange themselves in a stance that leaves no questions: onward only through battle.

The bestiary records the Lair Warden as a gate between the world of the living and a place where the sea keeps its own law. Defeating it is not the end of the road - it is an invitation to meet what the lair protects most.

The Lair Warden's tentacles scar the stone like mooring lines on a pier - proof it has held this gate for centuries. Defeat it and the whole archipelago hears a groan from the deep, a tremor fishers blame on the Heart waking to face you.

The Heart of the Kraken beats slowly, yet each pulse shakes the entire cave like a wave striking cliffs during a storm of the century. It is an ancient being long tied to legends of maritime catastrophe, sunk fleets, and nights when the sea burned with light.

It is not merely a monster. It is a symbol that the ocean has boundaries, and those who cross them without respect pay a price greater than gold. Its tentacles surround the chamber like walls of a living temple altar.

Defeating the Heart of the Kraken is an act that will long be sung in port taverns - songs whispered, because even victors know the sea remembers. The bestiary closes this entry with a sentence captains repeat: "We won the battle, but the sea never stops watching."

Kraken Slayers say pearl beds bloom overnight after the Heart falls, then vanish by the next moon. The lair's collapse is a myth, but tides around the archipelago run strange for a season - proof the ocean keeps score when its oldest tenant is humbled.

The Deck Rat guards the outer gate of Blackbeard's Fortress like a stray dog that learned to bite. He was pressed into service after stealing biscuits from the captain's table and survived only because he could climb rigging faster than anyone on the crew.

His cutlass is chipped and his coat smells of tar and cheap rum, yet he fights with the desperation of a man who knows the fortress has no room for failures. Pirates say he never sleeps on watch - he simply waits for someone foolish enough to test the first wall.
Defeating the Deck Rat is the first sign that Blackbeard's stronghold is no abandoned ruin. It is a living war machine where even the lowest deckhand fights as if the captain's eye were upon him.

Recruits in Tortuga dare each other to steal a chip from Blackbeard's outer wall - the Deck Rat collects those chips as trophies. His gate is the fortress threshold; pass it and the Powder Monkey's corridors smell of fear and black powder all the way to the captain's hall.

The Powder Monkey carries gunpowder through corridors where a single spark could end a dynasty of pirates. He is young, quick, and terrified in equal measure - a dangerous combination in a fortress full of cannons and grudges.
Barrels strapped to his back rattle with every step, and his hands are stained black from hauling charges to the battlements. Veterans treat him as expendable; the fortress treats him as essential.
The bestiary warns that underestimating a Powder Monkey is how fortresses stay defended. He may look like a boy, but in these halls a boy with powder is as deadly as a captain with a fleet.

Fortress manuals (stolen from a dead quartermaster) warn: never chase the Powder Monkey - lead him toward a spark and the wall wins. He runs the powder routes Blackbeard's cannons still feed on; beat him and sharpshooters above start taking aim - the fortress escalates.

The Cutlass Corsair patrols the torchlit corridors with the steady rhythm of a man who has fought a hundred boarding actions and lived. His blade is curved like a question mark, and he answers every challenge the same way - with steel.
He wears no fancy insignia, only scars and a belt heavy with trophies taken from intruders. In Blackbeard's Fortress he is the standard by which all other fighters are measured.
Captains who survived him say the Cutlass Corsair never speaks during battle. He lets his sword do the talking, and it has a vocabulary wide enough to end most conversations permanently.

The Cutlass Corsair's notches number over two hundred on a blade displayed in a Nassau museum - allegedly copied from the original. He holds the mid-fortress line where boarding tactics are taught; fall here and you never smell the treasury or hear Blackbeard's fuse-lit laugh.

The Sharpshooter watches from the battlement walls, musket ready, rain sliding off his tricorn like water off a ship's hull. He was once a navy marksman who defected for gold and never looked back at the uniform he burned.
One shot from his position can turn a confident assault into a retreat. He knows every angle of the fortress walls, every crack in the stone where wind carries the smell of the sea.
The bestiary records that fighting the Sharpshooter is a lesson in patience. In the fortress you do not charge blindly - you move when he reloads, or you do not move at all.

Sharpshooter nests are marked on fortress raider maps with skulls and 'reload counts.' One musket guards the approach to the boarding axeman's iron gate - survive the shot and the Quartermaster's Guard knows your name before you arrive.
The Boarding Axeman blocks the iron gate with a weapon made for breaking doors, masts, and men. Chains hang from his belt like trophies from ships that never escaped Blackbeard's reach.

His strikes are slow but devastating, each blow echoing through the corridor like a hammer on a hull. He does not chase - he waits until you come to him, and then the fortress itself seems to swing the axe.

Old raid logs say the Boarding Axeman was once a shipbreaker who joined the crew after Blackbeard sank his employer's fleet. Now he breaks invaders instead of timbers, with the same professional calm.

The Boarding Axeman's chains once hung from Blackbeard's flagship - salvagers paid gold just to touch a link. He guards the treasury approach; defeat him and the Iron Hook Veteran sends word (so say deserters) that Blackbeard should finish his drink.

The Quartermaster's Guard stands before the treasury hall with keys that jingle like a warning bell. His armor is polished not for parade but because the quartermaster demands order even in a pirate fortress.
He knows the value of every coin in the vault and the cost of every life spent defending it. To him, intruders are not enemies - they are accounting errors that must be corrected with violence.

The bestiary notes that defeating the Quartermaster's Guard means you are deep enough to smell the treasure. It also means the fortress will stop pretending you are a nuisance and start treating you as a threat.

Quartermasters in the Caribbean copied this fortress's ledger system - 'correct errors with violence' - from the Guard's own rulebook. Beat the Guard and the vault door sweats salt air; one hall remains before the Mutineer's Shade and First Mate Thunder.

The Iron Hook Veteran bears the scars of a dozen mutinies put down with one gleaming hand. His hook catches torchlight like a blade, and his banner - torn but never lowered - marks him as a man who survived what killed others.
He fought beside Blackbeard in the fortress's bloodiest years and stayed when lesser pirates fled. His loyalty is not to gold but to the legend that made this stronghold feared across the Caribbean.
Survivors say the Iron Hook Veteran fights as if remembering every comrade lost on these walls. The bestiary advises respect: he is not guarding a room. He is guarding a memory of war.

The Iron Hook Veteran's banner fragment sells on black markets as a charm against mutiny - it never works. He stands before the haunted lower halls where the Mutineer's Shade roams; veterans salute him even in death before marching to Thunder and Blackbeard.

The Mutineer's Shade drifts through fog in the haunted lower halls, a pirate who turned on his captain and was hanged from the fortress gate - yet never quite left. His eyes glow with cold light, and his voice is only the whisper of chains.
He attacks without warning, appearing where torchlight fails and courage thins. Many intruders flee before striking a blow, convinced the fortress itself has risen against them.
The bestiary records the Mutineer's Shade as proof that Blackbeard's Fortress remembers betrayal. Defeating him is not just a battle - it is a verdict against the ghosts of failed revolts.

Mutineer's Shade sightings spike before every failed fortress raid - superstition or warning, captains debate over rum. Clear the Shade and the antechamber lights burn steady for the first time in years, a sign First Mate Thunder has loaded both pistols.

First Mate Thunder stands in the antechamber to the captain's quarters, twin pistols drawn, coat heavy with medals taken from enemy ships. He is the second voice of the fortress and the last wall before Blackbeard himself.
His nickname comes not from weather but from the sound his shots make in enclosed stone - a crack that deafens, then silences. He has buried more captains than most pirates have met.
The bestiary warns that First Mate Thunder does not negotiate, retreat, or boast. He simply fires, reloads, and fires again until either he falls or the intruder does. There is no third outcome.

First Mate Thunder's pistols have names in crew gossip: 'Last Argument' and 'Final Verdict.' He is Blackbeard's last living wall; beat him and the captain's chamber doors unlock with the smell of burning fuse - no more intermediaries, only legend.

Captain Blackbeard sits upon a throne of captured ship wheels and broken crowns, slow-burning fuses woven into his beard casting hellish light across the captain's chamber. He is not a myth exaggerated by sailors - he is the reason the myth exists.

His iron hook gleams sharper than any cutlass in the fortress, and his laugh shakes the chandeliers of stolen crystal. Legends say he made a pact with storm and fire; the fortress says he simply refused to die like ordinary men.

Defeating Captain Blackbeard is an act sung in taverns from Tortuga to Nassau - songs half-whispered, because even victors know the sea has not forgotten his name. The bestiary closes with words every raider repeats: "The fortress may fall today, but Blackbeard's shadow sails on every horizon."

When Blackbeard falls, fortress bells ring across the archipelago in stolen dreams - or so drunk captains claim. Fortress Raider titles spread; smugglers use the stronghold's collapse as cover for new routes, but every pirate knows his shadow still sails every horizon.

The Ash Deckhand guards the first staircase of the crater, wading through embers as if crossing a wet deck. He once handled rigging on Davy Jones's prison ship before lava stripped his skin and left only soot.

His steps are light, but every footprint leaves a burning trail - proof that the volcano remembers every intruder. He strikes fast with a charred belaying pin, testing reflexes before the deeper guardians judge your worth.

Dockhands in the archipelago spit when they speak his name, claiming he still whistles the bosun's pipe tune on windy nights above the caldera. A salvager's journal notes: 'First ash, then the bell - the volcano knows you came.'

Defeat the Deckhand and the stairwell's heat drops one degree - old pilots say that is the Herald's invitation. He is the threshold to Davy Jones's Volcano, the fourth dungeon of the archipelago chain where drowned debts catch fire.
The Magma Watch Sailor once stood night watch in the harbor where Jones's fleet vanished. In death he returned with lava veins and a voice hot as a forge.
He carries a melted alarm bell as a mace and strikes as if trying to wake the entire volcano. Every blow sounds like a signal flare to the Basalt Ripper and the Herald waiting at the crown.

Night watch logs from Jones's lost port describe a bell that rang underwater the night the fleet sailed into fire. Sailors bet that hearing it twice in the crater means the Herald already knows your name.

Beat the Watch Sailor and steam vents shift - a path opens toward the Boatswain's Flame Soul. The volcano dungeon grows louder here; captains say the archipelago's southern reefs glow red when this guard falls.
The Boatswain's Flame Soul is the ghost of an officer who punished every mistake. Fire consumed him during a mutiny, but his orders survived death.

He whirls over basalt with a burning lash, commanding the living to kneel as the dead once did. His discipline holds the mid-crater where lava rivers fork toward the Crater Drowned and the Ash Priest's altar.

Mutineers' confessions (confiscated in Nassau) mention a bosun whose lash 'burned without flame' on Jones's barge. Tavern gossip says he still counts lashes aloud - and stops at thirteen, Jones's unlucky number.
Breaking the Flame Soul snaps the first chain of Jones's discipline in this dungeon. Deeper down, the Burned Crew Wraith gathers the sailors he once broke - defeat him before they merge again.
The Basalt Ripper hatched in lava fissures like a predator carved from stone. Its claws split steel, and its armor cracks only where magma breathes beneath the shell.
It hunts by tremor, reading the ground instead of sight. It patrols the fissure maze where intruders lose direction before the Crater Drowned pulls them under.

Miners on the outer isles sell 'ripper scales' that smoke when lied to - fraud, mostly, but the bestiary confirms real scales hiss near the caldera rim. Fishers avoid the south reef when ripper tremors shake their nets.

Slay the Ripper and the crater floor steadies for one heartbeat - a window sailors use to reach the drowning pool. The Herald's Herald priests say the beast was Jones's hound, bred to keep debtors from climbing back out.
The Crater Drowned drags anchor chains fused with bone. He was a sailor who tried to flee Jones's sacrifice barge and was thrown into the boiling pit.
He rises from the molten pool eyeless, yet hears heartbeats through steam and ash. He holds the central pool where the Ravenous Salamander feeds and the Ash Priest watches rites.

A bottle note found in the archipelago reads: 'He pulled my mate under by the chain we shared.' Divers refuse the crater pool on the anniversary of Jones's pact - they say the Drowned counts names aloud.

When he falls, the crater surface stills for one breath - the Salamander's hunger wakes immediately after. Beat him to prove you are not running from Jones's debt; the Herald waits only for those who walk forward.
The Ravenous Salamander is an ancient beast fed on the souls of dead corsairs. Its throat glows like a furnace and every hiss sprays sparks.
It crawls across walls and vanishes into cracks to strike from another angle. This guardian cannot be beaten by brute force alone - it herds prey toward the Burned Crew Wraith's chamber.
Old sea charts mark this volcano with a salamander sigil older than Jones himself. Captains leave rum at the crater lip 'for the furnace tongue' - superstition, but raids succeed more when they do.

Defeat the Salamander and ash falls soft as snow - the Ash Priest's litany begins. You are three stages from the Herald; the archipelago trembles when this beast dies, and Jones's cursed ships report strange lights below.
The Burned Crew Wraith is a single shadow made from sailors who burned under Jones's banner. Dozens of voices speak in one whisper about betrayal and debt.
Fighting it feels like dueling a wall of smoke that remembers every death. It blocks the ascent to the Ash Priest, merging and splitting to surround intruders who hesitate.
Survivors of the prison ship fire describe singing from the smoke - not hymns, but a muster roll of the dead. The bestiary lists their names when you win; lose, and your name joins the chorus.

Tear the Wraith apart and the altar stairs clear - the Ash Priest conducts rites for the Lava Leviathan and the Herald. This stage separates cowards from captains who earn the Volcano Conqueror whisper across the archipelago.
Jones's Ash Priest conducts rites on a basalt altar where lava serves as incense. He believes every slain soul strengthens his master's throne.
He casts ash like a curse while runes ignite beneath his feet with the names of the dead. He summons the Lava Leviathan when intruders reach the caldera crown's lower lip.
Confessionals seized from a sunken chapel quote the Priest: 'Jones eats what the sea rejects.' Pilots mark his altar on charts with a trident crossed by ash - avoid the rim during black moon nights.

Silence the Priest and the litany binding the volcano to Jones weakens. One beast and one Herald remain; beat him or the Leviathan rises twice as hungry, and the archipelago's tides run backward for a day.
The Lava Leviathan rises from the caldera like a warship forged in flame. Its scales are harder than iron, and its horns shatter basalt pillars.
The beast knows neither pity nor fear, only hunger. It is the final beast before the Herald - roars shake the chamber until ash falls like snowfall from the cavern roof.

Whalers passing the southern strait report seeing a fiery spine break the surface once per decade. They call it 'Jones's keel' and double their prayers - the bestiary confirms it dives back toward this caldera.

Slaying the Leviathan cracks the crown open to sky and hell alike. The Herald of Davy Jones stands beyond, trident in hand; conquer here and captains across the archipelago toast your name - if you return.
Davy Jones's Herald waits at the crater crown with a trident tempered in souls. He is the voice of the damned admiral and the final judgment for all challengers.
Each motion leaves a ring of fire, each word summons shadows from the ocean floor. He speaks verdicts Jones himself once pronounced against captains who cheated death.
The last page of a drowned captain's log reads: 'The Herald knew my debt before I spoke.' Volcano titles unlock when he falls; reef pilots say steam pillars rise visible from three islands away.

Defeating the Herald means the volcano names you conqueror - and the archipelago's southern routes open for a season. Jones's shadow remains on every depth sounder, but his gate here stays shut until another fool climbs the ash stairs.

The Reef Guardian stands where Atlantis meets the open sea, coral armor fused to skin that has not breathed air in millennia. He was sworn to Poseidon before the city sank, and his oath outlived the sun.
His trident does not strike first - it measures trespassers against the reef's patience. He tests footing and nerve at the palace gate where currents rip like boarding lines in a gale.

Pearl divers whisper that the Guardian counts heartbeats aloud - stop breathing wrong and the reef closes. A merchant's letter from Nassau mentions 'a trident shadow' guarding the richest bed east of Tortuga.
Pirates who defeat him earn the reef's grudging passage into Poseidon's Palace, the archipelago's deepest dungeon. Fail, and your keel joins the coral memorial the Avatar reads when judgment comes.

The Coral Warrior patrols shattered colonnades where Atlantean banners once flew. Shell pauldrons ring when he moves, and each blow carries the weight of a civilization that refused to kneel to the surface world.
He fights with the discipline of an elite guard who has trained since before your grandfather's grandfather was born. He holds the outer halls where Storm Sirens listen for intruders who bleed.
Atlantean coins (forgeries, mostly) show warriors with the same shell shoulders - collectors pay for them anyway. The bestiary notes his stance never breaks; only speed and cruelty together drop him.

Beat the Coral Warrior and colonnade echoes change - the palace stops pretending you are driftwood. The Storm Siren ahead sings for Poseidon himself; surface sailors say her note cracks masts ten leagues away.

The Storm Siren sings where palace currents collide with abyssal cold, her voice stitching lightning into tidal walls. Sailors who heard her on the surface went mad; intruders who hear her here go silent.
She does not beg for mercy - she offers the mercy of drowning quickly. Her song disorients before the Abyssal Executioner's chains find your throat.

Harbor wives in the archipelago warn children with 'the Siren counts waves' - one, two, three, then pull under. Captains plug ears with wax stolen from beekeepers; it helps until it melts in the palace heat.

Silence the Siren and the palace thunder fades to heartbeat rhythm - the Executioner waits in trenches below. Defeat her to prove your mind is yours; Poseidon's Herald records every victor's name in foam.
The Abyssal Executioner drags chains forged in trenches where light has never reached. He was Poseidon's answer to pirates who believed depth alone could hide them from divine judgment.
Each link remembers a condemned soul. His strikes feel less like combat and more like sentencing - until you prove your name is not yet written in the ledger of the deep.
Chain links salvaged near the palace sell as relics; the real ones still scream when heated. Smugglers call this hall 'the docket' - cases end in one swing.

Survive the Executioner and the Trident Keeper's golden gates gleam ahead. You are halfway through Atlantis's last dungeon; the archipelago's storms calm for an hour when he falls - then Poseidon watches personally.

The Trident Keeper guards the golden gates with rites older than any chart in Tortuga. His staff bears three prongs not for war alone, but for law, tide, and the price of entering a god's house uninvited.
Incense of brine and amber drifts around him like a second skin. He reads trespass without speaking - intruders feel weighed like cargo on a scale only gods see.
Priests of the tide isles copy his rites poorly, charging sailors for 'safe passage' that never works. The bestiary quotes him once: 'Gold buys a door, not forgiveness.'
Pass the Keeper and the Atlantean Champion salutes inside - honor before blood. Fail, and the reef remembers your ship; fishers will not sell you bait for a year.

The Atlantean Champion wears crystal armor grown from the palace floor, each facet holding a reflection of battles fought when Atlantis ruled the waves. He is the last knight of a throne room that never emptied.
He salutes before he strikes - an old courtesy from a world that believed honor could survive the flood. He guards the inner sanctum approach where the Tide Archmage bends water into weapons.
Arena fighters study recordings of his salute - some swear the crystal shows their own death if they watch too long. Surface kings once sent champions to duel him; none returned with titles.

Defeating the Champion breaks the first seal of the inner sanctum. Two guardians and the Avatar remain; the archipelago's pearl beds brighten when he falls, as if Poseidon turned his face toward the fight.

The Tide Archmage bends currents into blades and runes into whirlpools that swallow torchlight. He studied magic when the city still traded with surface kings, and he has not stopped learning in the dark.
His spells do not flash - they pull. Fighting him feels like dueling the ocean itself, one breath at a time, until you tear the tide from his hands.
Stolen spell pages circulate in Nassau, signed with a trident watermark - fakes, usually, but mages pay anyway. He mutters equations in a dead tongue; linguists say half the words are tide tables.

Break the Archmage and the Deepsea Leviathan coils free - no more illusions, only mass and teeth. Beat him to show Atlantis your mind cuts deeper than water; the Herald announces you to Poseidon next.

The Deepsea Leviathan coils through throne-room pillars broken by its own passage, scales black as the trench and harder than ship iron. It is not a pet - it is a living boundary between mortals and divinity.
When it roars, chandeliers of pearl tremble and gold dust falls like snow. It blocks the herald's stair - fleets would break here; one beast suffices.
Whalers who drift too east tell of a shadow longer than their ship that dives without sound. Charts mark 'Palace Leviathan' with a warning: do not harpoon unless you intend to sink.
Slay the Leviathan and pearl dust coats the hall like victory snow. The Herald of Poseidon descends to speak your name; one step remains before the Avatar judges the archipelago's boldest captain.

The Herald of Poseidon speaks with the sea god's authority, crown of foam and coral bright enough to blind unprepared eyes. He announces challengers to the throne as if the ocean were a court and every pirate a defendant.
His words can calm a storm or summon one. He reads charges - theft of pearls, murder of reef guardians, hubris - before the Avatar rises.

Court poets in the archipelago mimic his cadence at weddings and executions alike. Sailors say hearing 'You are summoned' in dreams means turn back; hearing it in the palace means it is already too late to run.

Defeat the Herald and the golden chamber opens fully - no more messengers, only the master. Win here and every island port hears your name tied to Atlantis; lose, and the reef grows one more coral figure with your face.

The Avatar of Poseidon rises at the heart of the golden chamber, divine trident leveled with the calm of a god who has drowned empires and forgotten their names. This is not a guard - it is the sea made judgment.
Each motion sends waves through the floor; each glance weighs your soul against the abyss. The palace dungeon exists to answer one question: does the surface world deserve the tides it steals?

When the Avatar falls, legends say Atlantis exhales and the archipelago's storms reorganize for a generation. Poseidon Slayer titles are born here - not given lightly, and never forgotten by the deep.

Defeating the Avatar means Atlantis names you champion - and the ocean remembers. Reefs bloom, currents obey strange new paths, and captains who were not there still toast your victory, afraid to sail without your luck.
